title: 2  Introduction to Ecological Economics
text:
2.2 Key Concepts
social metabolism
“The concept of a social metabolism is used in ecological economics and industrial ecology to capture the need of any human society for materials and energy, in the same way as any biological organism has a metabolism [see Chapter 11]. Order is created on the basis of using low entropy (Georgescu-Roegen, 1971), and the sources upon which humans are most dependent are stocks of concentrated minerals and the solar flow of radiant energy [Chapters 9 and 10]. Traditional societies relied on direct and indirect means of using the latter, with minimal use of the former. Modernity is built upon massive exploitation of the former.”

0.3 Assignments
The final assignment for this course is an essay answering one of these question:

Formulate a question you found difficult to answer previously, but now have the tools to reason around. Tie your answer to theory, practice, and concrete examples.
Reflect on the concept Barefoot Economics and its practical implications. Based on the course’s material and discussions, argue how your everyday behavior can contribute to “a safe and just place for all within planetary boundaries”. How can microeconomics and micropolitics influence larger systems? Use theory, praxis and examples to deepen your analysis.
Karl Polanyi’s work shows how tightly the economy, culture and society are intertwined. How have your own social and cultural background and experience formed your view on the economy? Point thoroughly to theories from the course to support your reflection.
Many believe that we lack holistic, comprehensive, and ecologically sustainable alternatives to capitalism which work at scale. How do you view this? Which economic system would be both realistic and necessary to meet the challenges we face?

Instructions: Write a 3000–4000 word essay with a clear structure, consisting of an introduction, a main body with well-developed paragraphs, and a conclusion. Cite correctly, following the department’s citation style. The library offers substantial support (use them!). Your arguments need to be coupled to the lectures, seminars, and assigned readings for this course. You are free to use additional material.

0.1.4 Using Computers and AI
Computers and AI are great tools and for better and worse there is no way around using them anymore. But you should be mindful about when they add to your learning and when they subtract from it.
I strongly encourage you to leave your computers—anything with a screen really—in your bags during class. Use pen and paper in class, then add a digital summary if you want to. It will help you stay focused and, more importantly, help others not to get distracted by whatever you would be doing on your screen. If you must use a screen, please find a seat at the back of the room.
I will not tell you what you should and should not use AI for; as long as it improves your learning outcomes. However, I think there are some elements you should consider. Since LLM’s entered mainstream use their abilities have grown tremendously. They can now carry out very complex tasks with high quality results. Making those decisions is an experience-based skill. But it still requires human knowledge and intervention to ultimately decide what is true, useful, effective, beautiful. The bad news: nobody is born with it, it is a skill that needs to be developed. Developing it requires annoying experimentation, failing and trying again and again, and reflexivity to develop. The good news: because of that it is something that will make you stand out if you have developed it.
You can use LLM’s to develop those skills too. They can even be extremely helpful for this: you can use them as a tutor testing your knowledge, or as peers to whom you explain concepts you are learning, or as guides helping you understand dense academic text by rephrasing it. But your learning success will depend on the same factors as with all other learning activities:

Make a plan of what you want to understand: what do you think will happen? Did it happen? Why, why not? Applied to AI: before asking the AI think about what you believe the answer will be. Was it?
Spacing is better than cramming: LLM’s generate a lot of text—fast. This can make it tempting to rush from topic to topic, question to question, but your brain needs time to memorize. Active recall—where you try to actively remember information instead of just passively consuming—spaced out over time is the key to remembering things. Applied to AI: take frequent breaks; ask it to quiz you on something you learned yesterday, or last week. Do not just reread old text passively.
Actively integrate new knowledge with what you already know. Test yourself to identify gaps in your knowledge. Try to fill them. Then test yourself again.

The central element in all of this is using your brain actively not just passively consuming information.

title: 2  Introduction to Ecological Economics
text:
By the end of this lesson, the students will be able to outline ecological economics as a field of research and teaching.
Students will be able to describe historical economic growth, its benefits and environmental drawbacks.
Students will be able to list course objectives: building vocabulary to interact with economic topics, describing ecological economics as a subfield, applying ecological economics concepts to analyze contemporary issues, evaluating economic proposals to address environmental issues, be able to design alternative approaches to environmental issues on ecological economic grounds.

title: 2  Introduction to Ecological Economics
text:
2.4 Notes
Before embarking on what this course covers, we need to accept the things it cannot cover: This course is not a general introduction into economic theory. For better and worse, it will not provide you with an (mainstream) economics eduction. You will not learn to think like an economist educated at an economics department, nor will you develop a deep understanding of the theories and economics degree would teach you, or be able to apply their tools and methods.
Ecological Economics as a transdisciplinary field.

title: 3  Principles of Ecological Economics
text:
Students are able to describe mainstream economic concepts (markets, economic growth, IPAT identity), and list their main advantages and shortcomings.
Students can describe foundational elements of ecological economics (stocks, flows, systems thinking, complexity, embeddedness).
By the end of this lesson, students are able to judge different economic relations to environmental issues regarding their human-nature relation, underlying assumptions, and consequences for ecological sustainability
